newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebels tighten grip on Zaire's mineral backbone.
newsitem.headline: Rebels tighten grip on Zaire's mineral backbone.

text.p: Zairean rebels tightened their grip on the country's economic backbone on Monday, appointing a new governor and announcing plans to renegotiate mining contracts with foreign firms.
Rebel boss Laurent Kabila appointed a provisional governor, Gaetan Kakudji, to oversee mineral-rich Shaba province, rebel officials in the provincial capital announced.

The move stalled an attempt by the incumbent, fiercely pro-autonomy Kyungu wa Kumwanza, to stay in power under the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL) rebels, who now control over half of Zaire.

Kyungu was sacked by President Mobutu Sese Seko in 1985 and reappointed last month ahead of the arrival of Kabila's rebels. Many Mobutu opponents in Shaba said allowing Kyungu to stay in power would be tantamount to letting him steal their revolution.

An alliance spokesman said elections would be held in Shaba at a later date, telling a news conference there was confusion and the alliance felt it was "not appropriate to go into detail on what's going on".

Kakudji, the new governor, said the alliance was committed to establishing a "social market economy" that would attract foreign investors and let the people of Shaba benefit from the wealth that Mobutu's regime had plundered for the past 30 years.

Rebel financial commissioner (finance minister) Mwana Nanga Mawampanga told reporters the AFDL planned to renegotiate contracts with international mining companies, including South African diamond giant De Beers Consolidated Mines.

"In the short-run, we are telling them that they can continue to work in the framework of the present arrangements. A bad contract is after all better than no contract at all," Mawampanga told a news conference.

"But at some point we are going to look at the fine print and make sure that we improve contracts where they can be improved...In other words we want to renegotiate in good faith to improve these contracts wherever possible."
He said he was not happy with the monopoly position of De Beers in the diamond industry.
"It is a monopoly and we don't want monopolies in this country anymore.
"If they don't want to accept that, they will have to make up their own minds what to do. We will not tolerate monopolistic behaviour in this country," Mawampanga said.
De Beers announced earlier this month its representatives had met Kabila for discussions which it said had focused on the security of its staff and facilities.
The firm has buying offices in the rebel-held towns of Kisangani and Mbuji-Mayi and a contract to buy the production of the Miba mine at Mbuji-Mayi.
Miba is 80 percent owned by the Zaire government with Sibeka of Belgium owning the remaining 20 percent. De Beers holds 20 percent of Sibeka and so has a minor indirect stake in the Miba mine.
